This atlas is a compact reading aid for the full
[Proximal-to-Distal Energy Transfer technical monograph](proximal_distal_energy_transfer/index.html).
It does not replace the monograph, adjudicate scientific consensus, or turn a
model result into a statement about golfers. Each source claim, reported status,
model domain, uncertainty boundary, and source-stated falsifier below is projected
verbatim from the pinned claim authority. The explanations here and the fields
labeled **Editorial** interpret the questions and comparison designs; they do
not change the imported adjudication.

::: {.callout-warning title="Interpretation Boundary"}
The atlas supports critical review. It is not coaching, clinical, equipment,
participant-validation, or causal authority. **Unavailable** means no qualified
workflow is registered for this atlas card. It does not mean no relevant
software or study exists elsewhere. A later provider publication needs an
explicitly verified registration before the atlas can present it as available.
:::

## Read the Statuses Separately

**Source-Reported Claim Status** belongs to the imported monograph's
adjudication. A mathematical identity, one numerical program, and a hypothesis
have different evidential scopes even when their cards look similar. The source
revision identifies that monograph snapshot. **Critique Ledger Disposition**
and **Readiness Record** come from their separately maintained records; a
readiness entry based on manufactured data is not a human experiment.
**Registered Validation Release** and **Registered Workflow** report what this
atlas has qualified for use, not whether the source proposition is true.

For example, the timing card reports differences from one 30 ms model branch:
continuing rather than removing the selected torso, bilateral-arm, or
bilateral-wrist command changes the model's delivery-speed endpoint by
approximately $+1.223$, $-1.364$, and $+1.818\,\mathrm{m/s}$, respectively.
These are three separate branch comparisons. These rounded values match the
[registered artifact at the imported revision](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/85cce4d3307bb7ad3953d9fc6e583e370803515c/docs/research/proximal_distal_energy_transfer/data/rotating_base_torso_velocity_study.json).
Reading that artifact verifies the reported values; it does not rerun the
simulation or validate a golfer. In the wrist-command comparison, delivery-speed
and contact-work differences even have opposite signs, so an increase in one selected endpoint is not a
complete account of energy transfer.

## Match the Question to the Comparison

### A Common Endpoint Does Not Specify an Internal History

Matching one scalar, such as clubhead speed, leaves other terminal-state
components and earlier forces unconstrained. This allows different histories
to have the same selected outcome; it does not prove that every proposed
history is dynamically or physiologically feasible. Declare the endpoint map,
event and tolerance, then compare internal states, boundary work, loads and
robustness under the same definitions.

A same-state intervention asks a different question. It changes a specified
input after the model reaches a shared complete state. Activation, deformation,
and other memory variables must be included if the model has them. Removing a
command is not generally the same as instantly removing muscle or contact
force. Subsequent feedback responses belong to the declared intervention
policy; they must not be mistaken for independently held controls.

### Equal Force and Equal Wrench Are Different Conditions

For ideal point-force vectors $F_1,F_2$ applied at position vectors $r_1,r_2$
relative to one reference point, the total force and moment vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}
F&=F_1+F_2,\\
M&=r_1\times F_1+r_2\times F_2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Adding $d$ to one force and subtracting it from the other keeps $F$ fixed but
changes the moment by $(r_1-r_2)\times d$. The **complete wrench** is unchanged
only if that moment increment also vanishes, for example when $d$ lies along
the contact-separation line. Intrinsic contact moments, friction, unilateral
contact and force limits change the admissible family; they must be specified.

For the unrestricted point-force example with contacts at $\pm0.2\,\mathrm{m}$
on the $x$ axis, opposite $7\,\mathrm{N}$ increments along $x$ preserve the
wrench. The same increments along $y$ change its $z$ moment by
$-2.8\,\mathrm{N\cdot m}$ when applied positively at the negative-$x$ contact.
This is a model identity, not a measured hand-force distribution.

An internal force pair can have zero total power on an ideal rigid club while
the hands still carry different loads. Zero rigid-body work does not establish
zero muscle effort, tissue deformation, or metabolic cost. Bilateral wrench
sensors constrain contact allocation, but do not by themselves identify muscle
coordination. Wrench and velocity quantities must use compatible reference
points, frames and signs; [the virtual-power derivation in Modern Robotics](https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/5-2-statics-of-open-chains/)
explains their dual mapping.

### Coordinate Changes Preserve Physical Pairings, Not Arbitrary Fits

Write a force-only endpoint fit as $\tau=J^TF+r$, retaining the generalized
residual $r$. For an invertible coordinate change $q=S z$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_z&=S^T\tau_q,\\
J_z&=J_qS,\\
\tau_q^T\dot q&=\tau_z^T\dot z.
\end{aligned}
$$

The power pairing is unchanged. Unweighted least squares in the two coordinate
systems need not choose the same fitted $F$: scaling a generalized coordinate
changes the implicit residual weighting. In a nondimensionalized example with
two generalized coordinates and a scalar fitted force, set $J^T=(1,1)^T$ and
$\tau=(1,0)^T$. The least-squares force is $0.5$.
With $S=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$ it becomes $0.8$ if the new residual is again
unweighted; transforming the residual metric to
$\operatorname{diag}(1/4,1)$ restores $0.5$.

Thus coordinate comparison needs the same physical trajectory, consistent
covector and Jacobian transformations, and declared metrics. If the force fit
has multiple minimizers, an additional minimum-norm choice selects among them;
that choice is an allocation rule, not evidence that a biological system uses it.
Reconstruction closure alone does not identify the physical wrench. Power and
work also depend on the observer: compare them in the same observer frame;
do not confuse coordinate invariance with observer independence. Likewise,
projecting along a path tangent $v/\|v\|$ requires nonzero velocity; at zero
speed a separate convention is needed.

### Support and Shaft Conditions Belong Inside the Energy Account

A stationary ideal support can exchange momentum while doing no work at its
fixed contact. A prescribed moving base can exchange energy through its
reaction force and velocity. Replacing either with a finite-mass dynamic base
changes the equations and admissible states. A fair comparison maps compatible
initial conditions and accounts for all boundary power; it does not assume
that changing the base automatically eliminates a negative club couple.

Internal storage matters as well as boundary power. For a linear spring with
displacement $y$ in metres and stiffness $k>0$ in $\mathrm{N/m}$,
$U=ky^2/2$ and $\dot U=ky\dot y$. The same nonzero deformation can be storing
or releasing energy depending on the sign of $y\dot y$. Peak stored energy therefore does
not specify the timing, destination or usefulness of returned energy. Damping,
actuation, contact, inertia and the selected endpoint all enter the comparison.

Use a **fixed-command comparison** to ask how outcomes change, or a
**matched-delivery comparison** to ask how required inputs and losses differ.
Keep the endpoint definition and event rule consistent. Imposing both identical
commands and identical outcomes may leave no feasible matched pair; forcing an
endpoint by an external constraint also changes the energy account. A rigid
reference model must state which masses, inertias and other properties were
preserved when compliance was removed.

## Interpret the Source-Stated Falsifiers Carefully

The source uses *falsifier* for several kinds of tests. Reconstruction or
convergence failures challenge a derivation or calculation. Different
same-state branch results challenge a registered numerical result. A sentence
that prescribes coaching breaches an editorial boundary. These are useful
checks with different meanings; passing them is not empirical confirmation.

Some imported wording needs further operational definition. In `PD-CLAIM-131`,
a successful simpler policy in a particular human study would challenge the
scope of the modeling guidance, not prove that all internal mechanisms are
identifiable from one endpoint. In `PD-CLAIM-068`, collecting extra contact
measurements does not refute underdetermination from the net wrench *alone*.
Unique identification requires assumptions or measurements that remove the
admissible nullspace. In `PD-CLAIM-144`, “reject the relationship” is not a
complete experiment: specify the relationship, comparison, measurable effect,
uncertainty and rejection criterion before collecting data.

The cards retain those source statements for traceability. The editorial
comparisons clarify what a useful test would need; they do not silently upgrade
the imported claims or imply that a proposed experiment has occurred. Evidence
artifact identifiers name the provider's files or external references and may
require inspection at the linked source revision.
